thread.title: Merger Activity At Historic High | Seeking Alpha

author: John M. Mason
title: Merger Activity At Historic High | Seeking Alpha
text:
M&A activity around the world hit $2.5 trillion in the first half of 2018, a historic high.
There had been evidence all along that records might be exceeded this year. And, there are indications that this record level will be maintained throughout the rest of the year.
And, the size of the deals exceeded all records: “Globally, companies signed 79 deals above $5 billion, surpassing the previous year to date record set in 2007. And a record 35 deals above $10 billion.”
Three reasons are given for all the activity: first, economic growth still seems to be quite adequate; second, there is a technological shift going on; and third, there are the Trump tax cuts and reform bill.
The biggest deals seem to be driven primarily due to technological disruption : “Technological disruption continues to be a big driver behind large M&A. Big shifts in technology are forcing companies across all industries to be creative and forge more strategic combinations. Adding in economic tailwinds and a continuing strong financing environment makes the current robust M&A market unsurprising.”
This is all a part of how the "modern corporation" is operating. Also, see my discussion of the latest of these transactions: “ Amazon.com and PillPack, Inc. ”
And, this is all connected with the fact that one of the major tools of the “modern corporation” is financial engineering. These organizations are not only advancing through mergers and acquisitions, they are enhancing their acquisition “currency” by the use of stock buybacks and higher dividend payments.
Right now, these three factors seem to be dominating some of the clouds on the future. Looming in the background are the rising short-term interest rates at the hands of the Federal Reserve System. Currently, the Federal Reserve officials have been signaling that there will be two more increases in its policy rate of interest this year, and this will be followed by three more increases next year.
This does not seem to be a disruptive factor right now and is built into current market rates of interest. But it is also true that many of these acquiring companies, like Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) and Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT ), have ample supplies of cash on hand to make their acquisitions or to engage in stock buybacks and high dividend payments to elevate the price of their stock.
Other companies engaging in acquisitions, like AT&T (NYSE: T ) seem to have no difficulty in issuing debt because there is ample money around and financial markets seem to be extremely liquid and longer-term interest rates are ridiculously low. The only concern with these companies is the issuance of too much debt.
In addition, there is concern over the regulation of these transactions. The Trump administration was against the recent AT&T deal but it still was approved by the court system.
Qualcomm (NASDAQ: QCOM ) has spent nearly two years trying to complete its takeover of NXP (NASDAQ: NXPI ) that is dependent upon the approval of the Chinese regulators.
It just seems that the regulatory road is not completely clear and there are some areas where unknown unknowns might exist.
Still, this does not seem to be a deterrent.
Finally, there is the fear of trade wars breading out. The Trump administration is the leading edge in the effort to impose tariffs against China and Europe and Canada and Mexico and other areas around the world and there are lots of evidence that these other places will respond in kind to whatever Trump and his team end up doing.
A trade war could disrupt a lot of things.
However, the M&A business continues at high levels and, in my view, will continue on for another six to eighteen months. It seems to me that there is just too much at stake for corporations to back off.
For one, their competitors are doing it. That means corporations cannot afford to be prepared to do their own deals in order to stay competitive. This is a part of the environment of credit inflation that governments have underwritten since the 1960s.
Governments want to keep their economies growing. Consequently, they plan fiscal and monetary policies to keep inflation sufficiently high enough. Two percent is the current rate of inflation built into the policy goals of the Federal Reserve System and other central banks around the world in order to keep unemployment low.
This means that the pressure is almost always on to support credit expansion. And, it is the expectation that the credit inflation will almost always be there that gives corporations the go-ahead to issue debt, to expand, to innovate financially, and to increase risk.
We saw this in the late twentieth century, we saw this before the Great Recession, and we have experienced it over the last ten years. This environment is built into the current mentality of the corporate world in the United States and pretty much through the developed world.
Secondly, we cannot underestimate the importance of this technological transformation of the scientific and the business worlds. We have seen a tremendous amount of change over the past thirty years or so, but the change that we have seen during this time is nothing compared to what is coming.
The technology companies are, of course, leading this charge. But, we have now seen that other corporations are catching on and becoming more of a player in the game. Even the banking industry seems to be coming out of their dream world.
This can only pick up steam. And, it will be worldwide.
But, there is one more thing that is, I think, impacting some of these transactions and that is the fear that the economic expansion is getting closer to being over. For one thing, the current economic recovery has just passed its ninth anniversary. We are now in the tenth year of the current recovery. It is one of the longest recoveries on record. So, how much longer can it go on?
Economists and other analysts are pointing to all sorts of possible trouble areas that could forecast a future downturn. One of the most predominant of these “signs” is the flattening of the yield curve . As many will tell you, if the yield curve inverts, this is a clear sign of an economic recession. An inversion of the yield curve has always been followed by a slowdown in the economy.
Just one other little fact. As mentioned above, the previous historical peak in the merger/acquisition data came in 2007. The Great Recession began in December 2007.
